questions.question: About 18% of Noted's events have no actor identity. An analyst proposes computing per-user activation on the 82% that do, with a footnote. What is the strongest objection?
options: 82% is below the coverage threshold required for any per-user metric
The footnote will be lost when the number is quoted in a review
The 18% is unlikely to be a random slice, so the remaining 82% is a biased population rather than a smaller one
The missing events should be assigned to a synthetic user so the total is preserved
questions.explanation: Events lose identity for structural reasons — signed-out sessions, public pages, system or integration writes — and each reason describes a kind of user or moment. Option B is a real risk and a weak objection: fixing the footnote does not fix the bias, and treating this as a communication problem is how the bias survives.

questions.question: Which missingness pattern should most strongly stop you from computing a per-entity rate at all?
options: A field missing at 3% for reasons nobody can explain
A field missing at 18% because public page views carry no actor
A field missing at 25% for signed-out sessions only
A field missing at 12% because an integration writes on behalf of an account
questions.explanation: A known structural reason gives you a nameable direction of bias, which you can exclude or model. An unexplained gap has unbounded direction and size, even at a low rate. Option C is tempting because 25% is the largest number on the list — but size is less dangerous than unknown shape.

questions.question: Meeting type is not captured anywhere in Noted's event data. A PM files a ticket to add a `meeting_type` property to document events. What is missing from this plan?
options: A backfill job to populate the property for historical documents
A decision about whether Noted has a product concept of a meeting at all, which must exist before anything can be typed
A privacy review of the new property
Agreement from the account manager on the list of meeting types
questions.explanation: You cannot instrument a concept the product does not represent. The gap is a product modelling decision wearing a data costume. Option A is the answer of a PM who understands backfills but not the sequence: there is nothing to backfill from, because the distinction was never observed.

questions.question: Noted starts recording a new field today, and the metric that uses it needs a fourteen-day window. The enterprise decision is being asked for this week. What follows?
options: Ship the field and report a preliminary reading in a few days
The decision should wait until the data is available, since deciding without it is guessing
The earliest defensible reading is at least two weeks away, so this week's decision must be made on other evidence or deliberately deferred
Backfill from document timestamps to approximate the missing history
questions.explanation: Instrumentation has no history, and the window sets a floor on when an answer can exist. Option B is the disciplined-sounding trap: it converts a data constraint into an indefinite hold, when the real choice is to decide on other evidence or to defer explicitly with a date.

questions.question: A team writes a complete tracking contract: every event named, every identifier specified, timestamps and stitching rules stated, missingness monitored. What can this still not deliver?
options: Consistent counts between two analysts querying the same table
Detection of an event that changes meaning after a UI change
A stable population definition across releases
Why a user did something, or whether the action was worth taking
questions.explanation: A contract makes data checkable, not meaningful. Intent and value are outside what any instrumentation records. Option B is tempting because semantic drift is a genuine failure — but that is exactly what a contract with a stated event definition and an owner is built to catch.
